thread.title: More Bites On Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Kwan-Chen Ma
title: More Bites On Apple - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
By K C Ma and Bilal Hashmi
For the better part of 2018, Apple shareholders were led to believe that Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) was immune by the tariffs as promised by President Trump. Therefore, it was to their surprise that Apple CEO Tim Cook would cut Q1 revenue guidance, citing poor iPhone sales in China. Cook's rare move ignited a widespread worry of a trade war-induced recession. The fear of recession was further confirmed by Samsung Electronics' (OTC: OTC:SSNLF ) guidance of a lower quarterly operating profit for the first time in two years, as a slowing Chinese economy also erodes demand for its chips and handsets. As simultaneous weaker guidance from the world's two largest makers of smartphones and semiconductors adds to worries for investors already on edge, it also points out the possibility that how China's current slowdown can quickly proliferate through the global demand chain. In this post, we look into this possibility.
China Relevance First, we want to examine how important China is to Apple. Historically, iPhone revenue represents close to 60% of Apple's revenue, and historically Apple's revenue comes from five geographical segments: Americas (45%), Europe (28%), China (12%), Japan (8%), and the rest of the world (7%) (Figure 1 and Figure 1B). China has not been a major player until 2014 when its revenue contribution reached $12 billion and 20% of iPhone revenue worldwide (Figure 2).
(Note: "1509": September 2015)
The Bad News Furthermore, if adding the rest of Asia to the Greater China segment (China, Taiwan, Hong Kong), the "Asia influence" (not counting Japan) cannot be underestimated because it would account for close to 30% of Apple's revenue. However, other than its growing size, China's presence becomes even more relevant as the economies in the rest of the world become increasingly more correlated with China's economy. Therefore, China's recession will not be confined in China.
The real bad news is that, if China' slowdown was to blame for Apple's downside guidance, the damage to Apple's shareholders, close to $450 billion in two months already, will not be the end of it. Considering that Apple's China revenue growth has been increasingly correlated with Apple's Americas and Europe revenue growths in recent years (Figure 3), China's slowdown in iPhone demand may soon be transmitted to the U.S. and Europe. The negative impact on Apple's total revenue will be further compounded considering over 65% of revenue share between Americas and Europe (Figure 1B).
The silver lining of the high correlation on the downside is that Japan is the only Apple revenue source which counteracts with China revenue growth in a meaningful way (Figure 4), although Japan's revenue share, less than 7%, is the lowest one of the five segments.
Revenue Impact on Apple Stock Price To Apple shareholders, maybe the more important question is how the correlated revenue growths affect Apple stock prices. Using the above relationship, we were able to estimate the correlated impact on all five Apple segments in terms of their segment revenue growths and Apple share prices, assuming 1% drop in China revenue growth rate (Table 1). The way to read Table 1 is like this: For every 1% decrease in China revenue growth rate, Americas and Europe segments will lose -0.21% and -0.18%, and Japan will gain 0.10% instead. In short, 1% China revenue loss will result in Apple's total revenue loss about 1.52%. The corresponding stock price impact is that Apple stock price will drop $6.88 from Americas' loss in revenue but gain $2.74 from Japan's 0.1% gain in revenue. The bottom line is that the net impact on Apple's share price considering the correlated revenue growth between five segments is a loss of $5.30 for every 1% drop in China growth rate.
When Tim Cook lowered the Q1 revenue guidance from the original $89-$94 billion range to $84 billion, or approximately a 6% reduction, he cited the miss was mainly due to China's revenue loss. Given that China has a 1.52 total revenue multiple, a 6% total revenue loss is equivalent to about 4% China revenue loss. Using an optimistic assumption that the Q1 miss is contained within the same quarter, Apple share price should have dropped by - $21 the day of the downside.
Incidentally, Apple stock price lost -$10.73 on January 2, amid Cook's announcement.
